detail.extracted_title: How the Tap Replaced the Banknote: Digital Payments Capture 89 Percent of Transactions Across Oman
detail.excerpt: From neighborhood coffee counters using smartphone terminals to instant transfers between friends, the Central Bank of Oman's latest national payment report shows how quickly everyday money in the Sultanate has moved off paper.
detail.article_html:
Stand at the counter of a bakery in Al Khuwair or a fruit stall in Nizwa at seven in the morning, and watch how people pay for a loaf of bread or a box of dates. Fewer wallets open for folded baisa notes. Instead, a card touches a reader, a phone screen lights up for half a second, or an instant mobile transfer clears before the bag is tied.

That quiet shift in daily habit now shows up in full across the Central Bank of Oman's National Payment Systems Annual Report for 2025. Digital payments accounted for 89 percent of all payment transactions by volume and 81 percent of their total financial value across Oman's banks and licensed payment service providers—leaving cash transactions handled through formal banking and payment channels at 11 percent of volume and 19 percent of value.

Nearly a Billion Everyday Retail Payments

The clearest measure of how ordinary households and shopkeepers move money lies in retail payment systems. Over the course of 2025, retail transaction volume climbed 53 percent to reach 974.19 million individual payments, carrying a combined value of OMR 47.80 billion—an increase of 24 percent over the previous year.

Instant mobile and bank transfers drove much of that momentum. Transactions processed through Oman's instant payment system nearly doubled within twelve months to 339.36 million transfers. Their total value rose 88 percent, jumping from OMR 5.56 billion in 2024 to OMR 10.45 billion in 2025 as families, freelancers, and small merchants increasingly treated real-time digital transfers as their default way to settle everyday bills.

At the institutional end of the economy, Oman's Real-Time Gross Settlement (RTGS) system—the backbone for high-value interbank and corporate settlements—processed OMR 269.23 billion during 2025, marking 12 percent growth compared to 2024.

The Rise of the Maal Card and Smart Terminals

Behind the convenience of a half-second tap sits a series of domestic infrastructure upgrades rolled out during the year. Foremost among them was the launch of “Maal,” Oman's national bank card, built to strengthen domestic payment sovereignty and lower processing costs for local merchants and consumers alike.

At the same time, the Central Bank expanded electronic Direct Debit Mandate services—giving businesses and households a reliable digital alternative to paper checks—and widened the use of the International Bank Account Number (IBAN) standard to cover domestic transfers alongside cross-border Gulf and regional payment links.

Across storefronts, the hardware of commerce changed just as noticeably. Point-of-sale (PoS) machines and SoftPoS solutions—which turn an ordinary smart device into a contactless card reader without bulky equipment—expanded by 18 percent compared to 2024, bringing the national network to nearly 120,000 active terminals. Small businesses, delivery drivers, and home-based Omani enterprises can now accept card and wallet payments wherever they meet a customer.

Sixfold Growth in Tokenized Security

One figure in the report stands out above the rest: transactions secured through payment tokenization grew by more than 600 percent in a single year. Rather than transmitting a customer's actual card number during a tap-to-pay or mobile wallet purchase, tokenization substitutes an encrypted one-time digital credential, pairing faster checkout speeds with stronger protection against fraud.

Taken together, the numbers sketch an economy steadily retiring friction from daily trade. Whether settling a OMR 269 billion institutional ledger or splitting dinner over a phone transfer, Oman's payment rails have grown faster, safer, and unmistakably local.

detail.instagram_caption:
Watch the morning queue at a neighborhood bakery or coffee shop anywhere in Oman, and the shift is unmistakable: folded banknotes and paper checks have largely given way to a half-second card tap or an instant mobile transfer.

According to the Central Bank of Oman's National Payment Systems Annual Report, digital payments now capture 89 percent of total transaction volume and 81 percent of total value across banking and payment channels. Retail payment volume jumped 53 percent to 974.19 million transactions worth OMR 47.80 billion, while instant transfers nearly doubled to 339.36 million operations—climbing 88 percent in value to reach OMR 10.45 billion.

Behind those everyday habits sits a modernized domestic financial backbone: the rollout of Oman's national "Maal" bank card, domestic IBAN integration, nearly 120,000 active PoS and SoftPoS smart terminals across local merchants, and a surge of more than 600 percent in encrypted tokenized wallet transactions.

Read the full analysis at omanspire.om (link in bio).
